title: Publish an RSS Feed of Your Content

chapters.title: Publish an RSS Feed of Your Content
chapters.subtitle: Let readers follow a list without visiting your site

steps.text: People can follow a site without visiting it, by adding its feed to a feed reader. In this video, you enable the Feeds feature, check that Lists is enabled, find the feed of a list, open it, and choose what it holds.

chapters.title: How feeds work
chapters.subtitle: Feeds, Lists and the feed of a list

steps.text: A feed is a page made for programs, listing the newest entries of a site. A feed reader checks the feeds a person follows and shows their entries in one place.

Two features work together. Feeds builds the feed in the RSS format and serves it, but publishes nothing by itself. Lists provides the lists whose items fill a feed, such as the posts of a blog, and gives each list its own feed settings.
A list feed starts with the title, the address and the description of the list. Then come the items of the list, newest first by creation date, up to a number you choose. Only published items appear.
The page of a list carries a link to its feed. Browsers and feed readers can use that link to find the feed from the page. The feed settings of the list control this link.
Feeds and Lists are separate features. Let's open Tools, Features, and type Feeds in the Search box.
Feeds is listed under the Content category. Click Enable, and a message confirms that the feature Feeds was enabled.
Lists is under Content Management, and it shows the Enabled badge, so there is nothing to do. Both features must be enabled before a list can have a feed.

chapters.title: The feed of a list
chapters.subtitle: Find the settings and open the feed

steps.text: To find the feed of a list, open Content, Content Items, and edit the Blog. A blog is a list of blog posts.
The editor of the Blog has three feed settings. The first is a checkbox, Disable RSS feed link generation. Unchecked means the feed is on.
A hint under Feed proxy Url shows the current address of this feed. Click it, and the feed opens in another tab.
The feed is a page of structured text, written for programs. A feed reader turns it into a list of entries. The page starts with the title, the address and the description of the Blog.
After that comes one entry for each published post, newest first. An entry has a title, a link, the body of the post, and the date it was published. A post saved only as a draft is not included.

chapters.title: Control the feed
chapters.subtitle: How many items, where it points, and when it is off

steps.text: In the editor, Feed items count sets how many entries the feed holds, and it starts at twenty. Let's change it to three.
The feed reads the published version of the Blog, so click Publish. When the feed is reloaded, it holds only the three newest posts.
Feed proxy Url takes a custom public address that proxies the local feed of the list. When it is set, the link in the page of the list points to that address instead.
To turn the feed off, publish the Blog with this checkbox checked: Disable RSS feed link generation. The page then has no link, and the feed address no longer returns a feed.

steps.text: Feeds builds the feed, and Lists supplies its items. Enable both, set the options on a list, and publish it. Thanks for watching.
